\section[caput]{caput — the head, still working two thousand years later}

\label{lesson:LA-C08-caput}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Few Latin words stayed as busy in English as this one. And yet — one of Latin's own descendants \textbf{abandoned} it for the actual body part.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{caput, capitis} — "\textbf{head}." A perfectly ordinary noun, and one of Latin's most productive exports:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{cap}tain & the "head" of a ship or unit \\
\textbf{cap}ital & the "head" city, or the "head" sum of money \\
de\textbf{cap}itate & to remove the head \\
\textbf{cap}itulate & to arrange terms under "little-head" headings — hence, to yield \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish kept \emph{caput} as its everyday word too: \textbf{cabeza} descends from it (by way of Vulgar Latin \emph{capitia}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
French had \emph{caput} available — and \textbf{dropped it} for the body part entirely. Instead French says \textbf{tête}, from Latin \textbf{testa}, "an earthenware pot, a shell." Roman soldiers joked about the skull the way English speakers say "noggin" (a small mug), and in Gaul, that joke eventually \textbf{replaced} \emph{caput} as the everyday word. \emph{Caput} didn't disappear from French, though — it survives there too, just not for the actual head: \textbf{chef} ("chief"), \textbf{chapitre}, \textbf{capital}, \textbf{capitaine}.

So three languages took three different paths with the very same word: \textbf{Spanish} kept \emph{caput} as the plain, everyday "head"; \textbf{French} demoted it to "chief/chapter/capital" and reached for a pot-joke instead; \textbf{English} never used it for the body part at all, only for these borrowed "head of something" senses.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "caput, capitis" — head{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the English family — "captain, capital, decapitate, capitulate"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the twist — French swapped \emph{caput} out for \emph{testa}, "pot"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{caput} mean, and what English words come from it? (\textbf{"Head"} — \emph{captain, capital, decapitate, capitulate}.) Did every Romance language keep it as the everyday word for "head"? (\textbf{No} — Spanish did (\emph{cabeza}); French replaced it with \textbf{testa}, "pot," soldiers' slang for the skull.) Where does \emph{caput} survive in French, if not as "head"? (\textbf{Chef, chapitre, capital, capitaine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[manus]{manus — the hand, and a famous grammatical exception}

\label{lesson:LA-C08-manus}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Here's a word that's productive in English \emph{and} grammatically odd in Latin itself — an oddity that then rode straight through into Spanish.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{manus, manūs} — "\textbf{hand}." It belongs to Latin's \textbf{4th declension} — a group of nouns ending in \emph{-us} that runs \textbf{overwhelmingly masculine}: \emph{frūctus} ("fruit"), \emph{exercitus} ("army"), \emph{senātus} ("senate"), \emph{portus} ("port") are all masculine. \textbf{Manus is one of only a handful of exceptions} in that declension — feminine, alongside \emph{anus} ("old woman") and \emph{domus} ("house," though \emph{domus} is even messier: it mixes 4th- and 2nd-declension endings throughout its own paradigm) — for reasons tied to each noun's own ancient history, not a rule you could predict from the \emph{-us} ending alone.

That oddity didn't stay buried in Latin grammar books: Spanish's word for hand, \textbf{mano}, inherited \emph{manus}'s feminine gender directly — which is exactly why \emph{mano} is famously feminine despite ending in \textbf{-o}, the ending that signals \emph{masculine} in nearly every other Spanish noun. One small Latin exception, carried whole into a completely different pattern in a daughter language, centuries later.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{manual} & done by hand \\
\textbf{manufacture} & made by hand (\emph{manus} + \emph{facere}, "to make") \\
\textbf{manuscript} & written by hand (\emph{manus} + \emph{scrībere}) \\
\textbf{maintain} & hold in the hand (\emph{manū tenēre}) \\
\textbf{manage} & to handle \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What gender is \textbf{manus}, and is that typical for its declension? (\textbf{Feminine} — unusual, since the 4th declension runs mostly \textbf{masculine}; \emph{manus} is one of a few exceptions, alongside \emph{domus} and \emph{anus}.) What Spanish word inherited this exact oddity? (\textbf{Mano} — feminine despite ending in \emph{-o}.) Give an English word from \emph{manus}. (\textbf{Manual, manufacture, manuscript, maintain, manage}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
